objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the kinds of descents, best glide and the forces in a gliding turn, fly straight descents and descending turns from the right seat while talking a learner through entry, the stabilized descent and the level-off, and spot and fix the errors beginners make in them.
why: Descents are one of the four fundamentals, and every approach and landing is built from them [[24:62|AFH 3-1]]. Glides are flown close to the ground, in normal approaches and after engine failures, while the pilot's attention is mostly elsewhere, so the habits you build here have to be right and nearly automatic [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. The gliding turn is also where a beginner's powered-flight rudder habits can turn into a skid and a spin near the ground [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

warmup: Think first: your learner closes the throttle at 4,500 feet to practice a glide. The nose drops at once, the airspeed shoots 15 knots past best glide, and in the left gliding turn that follows the ball sits well to the right while the learner pushes hard on the left pedal. At 3,000 feet the learner yanks the nose up to level off and the airplane sinks another 60 feet. How many separate errors did you just watch, which one would you fix first, and what would you have said on the ground to prevent each one?

key_terms.def: The normal way to lose altitude, also called a cruise or en route descent, at the AFM/POH airspeed and power, with a target descent rate of 500 fpm [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
A nose-high, power-assisted descent used mainly to clear obstacles on approach to a short runway, at an AFM/POH airspeed normally no greater than 1.3 VSO [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
A high drag, high airspeed procedure for losing altitude quickly, flown as the AFM/POH specifies; it often includes turns [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
A controlled descent with little or no engine power; gravity keeps the airplane moving along an inclined path [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
Distance traveled compared with altitude lost. 10,000 feet forward for 1,000 feet down is 10 to 1 [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
The airspeed that gives the greatest forward distance for a given altitude loss in still air; it occurs at L/DMAX [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
The highest lift-to-drag ratio. Gliding faster or slower than the speed that gives it increases drag and shortens the glide [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
The speed that keeps the airplane aloft longest by losing altitude at the lowest rate; a few knots below best glide and seldom published [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
A stabilized, power-off descent at the best glide speed. Abnormal glides are those flown at any other speed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
In steeper turns the outside wing travels faster and makes more lift, so the bank keeps increasing unless opposite aileron holds it [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
Starting the level-off above the target altitude because of the airplane's downward inertia; about 10 percent of the descent rate is the AFH starting point [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
An anti-icing system that preheats intake air; best used to prevent ice, and set full on before closing the throttle when icing is suspected [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

chunks.title: What a descent is and why it is a fundamental

body.p: Straight-and-level, turns, climbs and descents are the four fundamentals. Every flying task is built from them, and moving on to advanced maneuvers before they are mastered hinders learning [[24:62|AFH 3-1]]. Preparing to land is a mix of descents, turns and level flight, and the final approach ends with a change from descent to level flight while slowing for touchdown [[24:62|AFH 3-1]].

Purpose, for the learner: a descent is a controlled, planned change from level flight to a descending flight path [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Glides have a specific operational purpose in normal approaches and in forced landings after engine failure. Because the pilot's attention is usually on other things while gliding, the glide has to be flown almost subconsciously, and because it happens close to the ground, accuracy and good habits matter especially [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

The physics you will explain on the ground. When forward pressure starts a descent, the angle of attack drops for a moment while momentum carries the airplane along the old path; lift becomes less than weight and the airplane starts down [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. As the path tilts down, part of the weight acts forward along the flight path, more so as the descent angle steepens. To descend at the cruise airspeed, power must come back as the descent is entered [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]] [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. In a glide that forward component of weight is what keeps the airplane moving; it acts as thrust [[1:99|PHAK 5-2]].

bullets: The energy view: to go to a lower energy state, reduce the throttle so thrust is less than drag, then use the elevator to decide where the loss goes. To descend at a constant speed, pitch down just enough to hold that speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].
When drag exceeds thrust, the pilot can let the airplane descend at a constant airspeed or slow down at a constant altitude [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

Where this Task stops: approach descents to a runway are taught in AI.VII.B (Normal Approach and Landing) and the power-off glide to a spot in AI.VII.O (Power-Off 180). This lesson stays on the fundamental: entering, holding and leaving a descent, straight and turning.

callout.text: Throttle sets how much energy you lose; elevator sets whether you lose it as height or as speed.

check.q: A learner asks why the airplane speeds up when she lowers the nose with cruise power still set. What do you say?
check.a: In a descent part of the weight acts forward along the path, so at the same power the airplane accelerates. To hold the cruise airspeed in a descent, power has to come back as the descent is entered [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]] [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

chunks.title: The kinds of descent and what to know for each

body.p: The AFH expects the pilot to know the power settings, the natural horizon pitch attitudes and the instrument indications that produce each type of descent [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. For you, that means having all three ready for your training airplane before the first descent lesson.

head: Descent
What it is
Key numbers and notes
rows: Partial power (cruise or en route)
The normal way to lose altitude [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
AFM/POH airspeed and power for a prolonged descent; target 500 fpm; preselect airspeed, pitch and power and keep them constant [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
Minimum safe airspeed
Nose-high, power-assisted; mainly for clearing obstacles on approach to a short runway [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
AFM/POH airspeed, normally no greater than 1.3 VSO; steeper than normal; if mushing or a high sink rate develops, a lot of power may be needed to accelerate [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
Emergency descent
A specific AFM/POH procedure for losing altitude fast [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
Generally high drag and high airspeed, for example idle power, landing gear down and flaps up, at a set airspeed; often includes turns [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
Glide
Little or no engine power; gravity keeps the airplane moving [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
Usually flown at best glide speed, the normal glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]

body.p: In this Task you will teach mostly the partial power descent and the glide. The minimum safe airspeed descent belongs with short-field approaches and the emergency descent with emergency procedures; brief them here so the learner knows the family, then point to those lessons.

callout.text: In piston airplanes, do not practice emergency descents for long: end the descent once it is established and stable, to avoid overcooling the cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

check.q: Your learner wants to know which descent the AFH calls the normal way to lose altitude, and what rate it targets.
check.a: The partial power, or cruise, descent at the AFM/POH airspeed and power, targeting 500 fpm with airspeed, pitch and power preselected and held constant [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

chunks.title: Entering a descent: power, pitch, rudder and trim

body.p: Partial power descent entry. Reduce power, then use pitch to hold the airspeed you want: to descend at constant speed, pitch down just enough to keep the desired speed. When the new descent is established, adjust pitch and throttle as needed to hold it [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. Preselect the airspeed, pitch and power combination and keep it constant [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
Glide entry, the AFH sequence [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]:

bullets: Close the throttle and, if equipped, move the propeller control forward.
Hold altitude with back pressure while the airspeed bleeds off to best glide speed.
Expect the nose to drop as soon as power comes off: less slipstream over the horizontal tail means less tail-down force. Counter it with more back pressure at the same moment.
This matters most in fast airplanes, which do not lose speed readily; any slight nose-down movement gives an immediate speed increase.
At best glide speed, set the pitch attitude to hold it, using the natural horizon and a quick look at the instruments.
When the airspeed has stabilized, trim away the control pressure. Precision at best glide is what delivers its benefit.

body.p: Rudder and control feel in the glide. The airplane's design compensates for P-factor and slipstream in powered flight. In a glide those effects disappear but the built-in compensation remains, so slight left rudder pressure is likely needed to stay coordinated. The controls also need bigger deflections because the airflow over them is slower [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

callout.text: Say it in this order in the air: power, hold the nose, wait for the speed, set the attitude, trim. Two listed errors come from skipping 'hold the nose' and 'wait for the speed' [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

check.q: Your learner closes the throttle and the nose drops 5° below the level attitude before the airspeed has decreased. Which AFH errors is this, and what should he have done?
check.a: Inadequate back pressure during glide entry, giving an overly steep glide, and not slowing to glide speed before lowering the pitch. Hold altitude with back pressure as power comes off, then lower the nose at best glide speed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

chunks.title: Best glide, L/DMAX and the cardinal rule

body.p: The glide ratio is the distance traveled for the altitude lost: 10,000 feet forward for 1,000 feet down is 10 to 1 [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Best glide airspeed gives the greatest forward distance for a given altitude loss in still air, and it occurs at the highest lift-to-drag ratio, L/DMAX [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
Above or below best glide airspeed, drag increases and the glide ratio gets worse [[24:83|AFH 3-22]]. Too slow and too fast both land short, which surprises learners who think 'slower is flatter'.

head: Factor
Effect on the glide
rows: Weight
Does not change the glide angle or distance if the right airspeed is flown; a heavier airplane must glide faster and gets there sooner [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Drag devices (flaps, gear, cowl flaps)
More drag needs a lower pitch to hold speed, which steepens the path; clean up to glide farthest [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Wind
A tailwind lengthens the glide over the ground and a headwind shortens it [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Minimum sink speed
Lowest descent rate and longest time aloft but less distance, for example before ditching; usually a few knots below best glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]

callout.text: The AFH calls this a cardinal rule: never try to stretch a glide by adding back pressure and slowing below best glide speed. It leads to landing short and can lead to a stall and loss of control [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

body.p: Abnormal glides, at speeds other than best glide, can mean missing the landing spot, flat approaches, hard touchdowns, floating, overruns and possibly stalls [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Teach the abnormal glide only after the normal glide is solid [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Spot landings from a glide are AI.VII.O's job.

check.q: A learner asks whether the heavier airplane on a dual flight glides a shorter distance than when she is solo. What is the answer?
check.a: No. At the right airspeed, weight does not change the glide angle or distance; the heavier airplane must glide at a higher airspeed and simply arrives sooner [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

chunks.title: Visual references: horizon, wingtips, sound and feel

body.p: Pitch: the descent attitude is set and held against the natural horizon, then checked on the instruments [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. The AFH tells the beginning pilot to memorize the glide attitude and speed against the natural horizon, along with the airflow sound, the forces on the controls and the feel of the airplane [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

Bank: in a descending turn the top of the cowling against the horizon gives a reasonable first indication of bank angle, then the instruments confirm it [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. In the straight descent, the wingtips confirm the wings are level; fixation on the nose is how a learner ends up with one wing low (a climb error on the AFH list [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]; application: the same fixation does it in a descent).

head: Airspeed reference
What the learner notices
rows: Sound
Rising sound level means increasing speed; falling sound means decreasing speed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Visual
The nose against the natural horizon compared with the memorized glide attitude [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Pressure
The control forces needed to hold the attitude; they are lighter at the low airspeeds of a glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]

body.p: Early on, a learner may not notice small changes in airspeed or bank by sight or by control pressure. When a change in sound is noticed, cross-check the visual and pressure references. Use all three consciously until experience builds, then stay alert to any change [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

Seat and posture still matter. Most airplanes have side-by-side seats, so from the left seat the nose appears to rise in a left turn and drop in a right turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. A learner who leans away from the turn loses the correct picture; correct it at once [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

callout.text: Have the learner close the throttle once at altitude with eyes outside and call out what changed: the sound, the nose, the yoke. Naming the cues is how 'feel' starts.

check.q: In a stabilized glide the learner hears the wind noise getting louder. What should she do first?
check.a: Treat it as increasing airspeed and cross-check the visual reference (nose against the horizon) and the control pressure, then correct pitch on the horizon [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

body.p: Use the integrated method: outside references and flight instruments together, with about 90 percent of attention outside on attitude and traffic [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] and no more than about 10 percent inside, in quick checks [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. Corrections are made on the natural horizon and then rechecked on the instruments [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

head: Instrument
What it confirms in a descent
rows: Airspeed indicator
The target descent or glide airspeed is being held; pitch is the correction [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Vertical speed indicator
The descent rate, for example 500 fpm in a partial power descent [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
Altimeter
When to start the level-off lead [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Attitude indicator, heading indicator, turn coordinator
Bank and heading in straight descents and the bank angle and coordination in turns [[24:76|AFH 3-15]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]
Engine instruments
RPM or manifold pressure, and cylinder head temperature in long idle descents if installed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]

body.p: The AIH says instrument references should start the first time each maneuver is introduced, and the control inputs are the same whichever reference is used [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. It adds that learners trained this way land better because their airspeed control is more precise [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], which is exactly the skill a stabilized descent builds.

callout.text: Chasing the airspeed indicator is a listed descent error, and so is trying to fly the glide solely by the instruments [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Set the attitude outside, wait, then check. Make sure the learner also knows this does not prepare them for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Your learner keeps the airspeed needle within 2 knots but only by staring at it and making constant small pitch changes. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
check.a: That is chasing the airspeed indicator and flying the glide by instruments alone, both AFH errors. Set the glide attitude on the natural horizon, let it stabilize and trim, then use brief instrument checks [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: Descending and gliding turns: pitch, overbanking and coordination

body.p: The AFH wants the instructor to explain why gliding turns are harder to coordinate than powered turns: no propeller slipstream or P-factor, less effective controls at low airspeed, and design corrections built in for powered flight [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Three things push the nose down and the glide speed up in a gliding turn [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]:

bullets: Less vertical lift, because the lift is tilted with the bank.
Too much rudder, applied because the control pressures feel lighter.
The airplane's normal stability, which noses it down with the power off.

body.p: So the gliding turn needs more back pressure than a straight glide or a level turn [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Rudder still counters yaw when rolling in and out, but with less pedal pressure than in powered flight. A learner who uses powered-flight rudder pressures overcontrols, and that causes slips and skids [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

Overbanking. In shallow turns (about 20° or less) the airplane tends to roll level unless aileron is held into the turn; in medium turns (about 20° to 45°) it holds the bank with neutral aileron; in steep turns (about 45° or more) it keeps rolling into the bank unless opposite aileron holds it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. The cause is the outside wing traveling faster and making more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. If the nose gets low in a steep bank, reduce the bank first with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose; elevator alone only steepens the bank [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

head: Hazard
How it develops
rows: Low gliding steep turn after engine failure
Rudder held into the bank while pulling to save altitude can quickly become an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Power-off approach, cross-controlled
Too much rudder banks the airplane; the pilot holds opposite aileron and pulls; a stall in that state almost certainly gives a rapid, unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]

body.p: Rolling out. Start the rollout before the heading; half the bank angle is the rule of thumb [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. When returning from a gliding turn to a straight glide, release the extra back pressure, or the nose pitches up and the airspeed decays [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Partial power descending turns: the sources treat climbing turns and gliding turns in detail but not powered descending turns; application: the same turn factors apply, with power available to hold the airspeed.

callout.text: Gliding turn: more pull, less pedal, steady bank, and let go of the pull on the way out.

check.q: In a 30° gliding left turn the ball is out to the right and the learner has a lot of left rudder in. What is happening and why is it dangerous?
check.a: A skid from excessive rudder in the direction of the turn, a common carryover from powered rudder pressures. With back pressure added it can develop into a spin, especially low [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

chunks.title: Leveling off: the lead, the power and the pitch

body.p: The airplane has downward inertia, so the level-off starts before the target altitude. The amount of lead depends on the descent rate and the airspeed wanted at the end [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

head: Situation
Lead
Technique
rows: Partial power descent at 1,000 fpm
10 percent of the rate: 100 feet [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
Raise the nose and add power to stop the descent and hold airspeed [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]
Practice glide at 500 fpm, ending faster than glide speed
About 100 feet [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Add cruise power at the lead point; the nose tends to rise as power and speed increase; control the pitch to finish at the altitude and airspeed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Simulated power failure training
Power at the 10 percent lead value [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Slow but positive power, raise the nose to stop the descent, retrim [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Actual complete power failure
Hold best glide until it is time to configure for landing [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Plan a steeper approach than usual; a 10 percent lead should be enough to slow the descent before landing [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]

body.p: After leveling, retrim as necessary [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]; whenever power, pitch attitude or configuration changes, the airplane needs retrimming [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]. In energy terms, the descent was AFH Rule #2: reduce throttle so thrust is less than drag, and pitch down just enough to hold the speed. The level-off is the last line of that rule: upon reaching the new energy state, adjust pitch attitude and throttle setting as needed to maintain the new path and speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]]. Holding a constant altitude and airspeed means thrust equals drag again [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

callout.text: Two level-off errors on the AFH list: inadequate pitch control during recovery from a straight glide, and too much rudder during recovery from gliding turns [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Watch the first three seconds after the power goes in.

check.q: Your learner is descending at 700 fpm in a partial power descent toward 3,000 feet. At what altitude should she begin the level-off, using the AFH 10 percent rule?
check.a: 10 percent of 700 fpm is 70 feet, so begin at about 3,070 feet, raising the nose and adding power to stop the descent and hold airspeed [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

chunks.title: Engine care in long descents: carburetor heat, cooling and mixture

body.p: Carburetor ice can form in any phase of flight, but it is particularly dangerous at reduced power in a descent, where it can build unnoticed until power is added [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. With the throttle closed, the engine cools quickly, fuel vaporizes less completely and the engine is more prone to carburetor ice [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

bullets: If carburetor icing conditions are suspected and closed-throttle operation is planned, set carburetor heat full ON before closing the throttle and leave it on during the closed-throttle operation [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Open the throttle smoothly for a few seconds now and then to keep the engine warm, or the carburetor heater may not make enough heat [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Carburetor heat reduces power, sometimes by up to 15 percent, because heated air is less dense [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Do not use it when full power is needed, as during takeoff, or in normal operation except to check for or remove ice [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]].
Follow the manufacturer's recommendations for its use [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

body.p: Engine cooling. In its steep spiral section the AFH warns that idling for a long time in a glide can cause excessive engine cooling, spark plug fouling or carburetor ice. Periodically advance the throttle and hold it for a few seconds, and watch the cylinder head temperature if the airplane has a gauge. Adjust pitch to keep the airspeed constant while the power is in [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. High-speed descents give the engine extra cooling air and can shock cool it with abrupt temperature changes [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].
Mixture. In a descent from high altitude the mixture must be enriched, or it may become too lean; monitor engine temperature and enrich as needed, using the AFM/POH method [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

callout.text: Make 'carb heat, then throttle' one motion in the learner's hands, every time conditions call for it, and brief what the RPM drop on carb heat looks like before the flight. Habits built at altitude are the ones that show up on a real approach.

check.q: On a cool, humid day the learner closes the throttle for a long glide and then reaches for the carburetor heat. Why is that the wrong order?
check.a: With carburetor icing suspected and closed throttle planned, carburetor heat goes full ON before the throttle is closed; the engine cools fast at idle, making less heat available and ice more likely [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

chunks.title: Demonstrating it from the right seat

body.p: The CFI ACS asks you to establish, maintain and level off from straight descents and descending turns (AI.VIII.D.S1) while you teach. When demonstrating, explain the power settings and attitudes as you fly, keep the demonstration in the same order as your explanation, and say at once if it strays [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
A talk-through you can adapt (each step from the sources):

bullets: 'Clear left, right, above and below, and gentle banks as we go down.' Clearing before the maneuver and during descents [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
'Carb heat on, throttle to idle. Hold the nose: hear the wind get quieter as we slow.' Glide entry and the sound cue [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
'Best glide on the airspeed. Now lower the nose to this picture on the horizon and trim.' Pitch on the horizon, then trim once stable [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
'A little left rudder to keep the ball centered with the power off.' [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
'Rolling into a gliding turn: a touch more back pressure, lighter on the rudder than you expect.' [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
'Rolling out: let go of that extra pull so the speed stays put.' [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
'100 feet to go: cruise power, hold the nose from rising, level, retrim.' [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]

body.p: Your sight picture is not the learner's. Pitch and bank references depend on seating position and the pilot sits off the longitudinal axis, so the nose picture changes in left and right turns [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Application: describe the learner's nose reference from the left seat rather than your own.

callout.text: Fly the demonstration to the precision you want copied; learners imitate the instructor's performance, including the safety steps such as clearing and carburetor heat [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

check.q: During your demonstration the airspeed runs 8 knots fast while you are explaining the gliding turn. What should you do?
check.a: Acknowledge and explain the deviation right away, since the demonstration should match the explanation; then show the correction on the horizon [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

head: Stage
Descent content
rows: Ground

The forces in a descent, the descent types, best glide and the stretch rule, the three gliding-turn factors, the level-off lead, carb heat; the outside pictures and instrument indications to expect [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Demonstrate
Straight glide, then a gliding turn, then the level-off, explained as you fly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, you fly
Hear whether the learner knows the entry order and the gliding-turn changes before they are busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner flies
Partial power descents first, then straight glides, then gliding turns both ways, then level-offs to a target altitude; sound and feel cues called out [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Debrief
Learner self-assessment first, then your assessment and concrete fixes [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

bullets: Teach the normal glide until it is solid, then show abnormal glides, too fast and too slow, so the learner sees the cost [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

Practice high. The AFH lists power-off gliding descents and descending turns among the slow flight exercises and wants slow flight completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL in a single-engine airplane [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. Application: use at least that height for plain glide practice too.
Use this Task's own distraction from the AIH list: have the learner climb 200 feet and hold it, then descend 200 feet and hold it [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

When safe, let the learner go part way into an error such as a skidding gliding turn at altitude, so they find the way out; safety permitting [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; when a recovery is needed, take the controls and announce it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
If the glide looks good but you doubt the understanding, have the learner vary it: different bank, other direction, a different target altitude [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Turns in only one direction is a listed turn error [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Alternate left and right gliding turns; the rudder need differs with the power off [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

check.q: Why does the AFH want the abnormal glide taught only after the normal glide is solid?
check.a: The learner needs a solid sense of the normal glide first; abnormal glides, too fast or too slow, are then compared with it to show missed spots, flat approaches, hard landings, floating and possible stalls [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

chunks.title: Risk: distractions, task priorities, awareness and disorientation

body.p: Distractions. Most stall and spin accidents happened when the pilot's attention was diverted; 60 percent were during takeoff and landing and 20 percent followed engine failure [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Application: those phases are full of the glides and descending turns of this Task. Glides are flown while the pilot attends to other details, so the mechanics must become nearly automatic [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

Task prioritization. Fly the airplane first. Practice tasks in isolation until each is done reasonably well before combining them; fixation is often a sign of too little isolated practice [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]], and budget time and prioritize tasks once airborne [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

Loss of situational awareness. Know where you are, your flight path and the traffic around you [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. A descent ends somewhere: a learner busy with the glide can lose track of terrain, airspace floors and the level-off altitude. Many accidents start with a minor distraction such as a gauge that is not reading right [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

Disorientation. A prolonged, coordinated descending turn is the graveyard spiral set-up. Without good visual references the pilot can feel level while descending, pull back to stop the descent, and tighten the spiral [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. A quick throttle reduction can also give a false sense of pitching down, so a disoriented pilot may pull up toward a stall [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

bullets: Teach the graveyard spiral on the ground with this figure. A false horizon can occur when the natural horizon is obscured [[24:65|AFH 3-4]]; application: practice descending turns where the horizon is clear.
Avoid head-down distractions mid turn; head movement in a turn can trigger the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
Keep the learner's attention on airspeed during gliding turns near the ground, where cross-control can lead to a spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

callout.text: If a spiral starts, roll the wings level before raising the nose; pulling with the bank in only steepens it [[24:77|AFH 3-16]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

check.q: Your learner, in haze, has been in a long gliding turn and says 'we're level, just sinking'. Why is pulling back the wrong fix?
check.a: That is the graveyard spiral illusion: in a prolonged turn the pilot may feel level while descending, and pulling back tightens the spiral and increases the altitude loss. Level the wings first [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

body.p: Failure to clear for traffic in the turn direction or in the descent is the first error on the AFH descent list [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Every pilot must keep vigilance to see and avoid other aircraft when weather permits, under IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113]].

bullets: During climbs and descents, make gentle banks left and right often enough to keep the airspace scanned continuously [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Avoid entering traffic patterns while descending [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Make clearing turns before a practice maneuver and have the learner call 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Rates of descent and closure leave little time to detect, decide and act [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].
An aircraft below the horizon is probably at a lower altitude, which is where a descending airplane is heading [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: Blind spots: wings and fuselage hide aircraft above and below, so move your head and lift a wing when needed to see [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]] [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. Traffic clusters near VORs and surface areas [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Most midair collisions happen in daylight VFR within 5 miles of an airport [[24:31|AFH 1-10]], and a study found most occur near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet, with a flight instructor aboard in 37 percent [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: In a high-wing trainer the wing hides the airspace into which a turn is going, and a descent goes toward traffic below. Make the learner own the clearing; learners who think you handle traffic never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: What does the PHAK say to do about traffic while descending in conditions where other traffic can be seen?
check.a: Make gentle banks left and right at a frequency that allows continuous visual scanning of the airspace [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

body.p: The AFH lists 13 common errors for descents and descending turns [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. For S2, the examiner may fly some of them while you watch; name the error, say what caused it and give the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Not clearing for traffic in the turn direction or descent
Turn or descent started with no look
Clear first, gentle banks during the descent [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Too little back pressure at glide entry
Nose drops as power comes off; overly steep glide
Add back pressure as the throttle closes [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Not slowing to glide speed before lowering the nose
Airspeed well above best glide after entry
Hold altitude until best glide, then set the attitude [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Flying the glide solely by instruments
Head down, attitude wandering
Attitude on the horizon, then a brief check inside [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Not sensing airspeed changes by sound and feel
Speed drifts with no reaction until the gauge shows it
Call out sound, visual and pressure cues [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Unable to stabilize the glide (chasing the airspeed)
Constant pitch changes, speed oscillating
Set the attitude, wait, trim, then check [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Stretching the glide with back pressure
Airspeed below best glide, nose rising to reach a spot
Hold best glide; slower lands shorter [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Slipping or skidding in gliding turns
Ball off center; powered-flight rudder pressure
Lighter rudder with power off; keep the ball centered [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Not lowering the nose at gliding turn entry
Airspeed decays as the turn starts
Lower the pitch slightly as the bank goes in [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Excessive rudder in the gliding turn recovery
Yaw or skid as the wings level
Smaller, coordinated aileron and rudder [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Poor pitch control recovering from a straight glide
Altitude lost or ballooning at level-off
Use the lead, add power, control the nose rise [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Cross-controlling in gliding turns near the ground
Rudder one way, aileron the other, back pressure added
Coordinated controls; airspeed first; no rudder to tighten the turn [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Not holding a constant bank in gliding turns
Bank creeping, nose wandering
Hold the bank on the cowling and horizon; opposite aileron if it steepens [[24:76|AFH 3-15]] [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct. When the learner thinks aloud you can tell whether an error is a misconception or a motor-skill problem [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Follow the learner's eyes: a long stare at the airspeed indicator suggests fixation, and eyes that never go to the engine gauges in a long idle descent suggest inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

Note a gap in the list: 'not lowering the nose at turn entry' and 'too much back pressure' look alike from the right seat. Application: if airspeed decays early in the turn, it is the entry; if it decays after rollout, it is the extra back pressure not released [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

callout.text: Rehearse the three-part answer for each error: 'I see..., because..., so we...'. It is what S2 asks for.

check.q: After rolling out of a gliding turn, the nose rises and the airspeed drops 10 knots below best glide. Which error is it and what is the fix?
check.a: The back pressure added for the turn was not released at rollout; decrease it as the wings level to re-establish the normal glide airspeed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

Right: a glass display with an airspeed tape, attitude display, altitude tape and vertical speed scale.

A box at the raised outer wing reads outer wing travels greater distance, higher speed, more lift. A box at the lower inner wing reads inner wing travels shorter distance, lower speed, less lift.

scenario.title: Gliding turns on a humid morning
scenario.setup: You are a CFI with a learner on the fourth lesson in a carbureted high-wing trainer. The plan is partial power descents, then straight glides and gliding turns from 5,500 feet, leveling off at 3,500 feet. It is a cool morning after rain, the air feels damp, and the practice area lies under the arrival path to a nontowered airport 6 miles away. Last lesson the learner flew level turns with heavy rudder.

questions.q: What do you brief on the ground about the engine before the first glide?
questions.a: Carb ice is particularly dangerous at reduced power in a descent; with icing suspected, set full carburetor heat before closing the throttle and leave it on, and open the throttle briefly now and then to keep the engine warm [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Long idle can also overcool the engine and foul plugs [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: How do you handle collision risk on this flight?
questions.a: Clear before each maneuver with the learner calling it, and make gentle banks left and right during descents to keep scanning [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Most midairs are near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet and an instructor is often aboard, so the learner owns the scan [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

questions.q: Given last lesson's heavy rudder, what do you expect in the gliding turns and how do you pre-empt it?
questions.a: A skid, because rudder pressures are lower with power off and a learner may use powered-flight pressures [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Brief 'more back pressure, less rudder' and show the ball in your demonstration.

questions.q: In the first glide the learner keeps the airspeed within 3 knots only by staring at the indicator. What do you do?
questions.a: That is chasing the airspeed and flying by instruments, both listed errors [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Have the learner set the attitude on the horizon, trim, and use sound and pressure cues with brief instrument checks [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

questions.q: Halfway through a 270° gliding turn the learner reaches down to find a chart. Why stop this?
questions.a: Head movement during a turn can cause the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]], and diverted attention is the classic set-up for stall and spin accidents [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Keep the distraction for straight flight.

questions.q: At 3,600 feet in a 500 fpm practice glide, the learner wants to level at 3,500 at cruise speed. What does the AFH say to do?
questions.a: Start about 100 feet above, at the lead point, add cruise power, control the nose as it rises, finish at the target altitude and airspeed, and retrim [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

skills.do: Establish, maintain and level off from straight descents and descending turns from the right seat while explaining: partial power entry, glide entry holding altitude to best glide, trim, the gliding-turn back pressure and lighter rudder, and the level-off with a lead. The CFI ACS gives no numeric tolerance for this Task, so hold airspeed, bank and the level-off altitude as precisely as you will expect of a learner.
skills.practice: Fly the talk-through aloud until talking costs you no airspeed. Practice level-offs at several descent rates and noting where you start the lead, and gliding turns both ways with the ball centered [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task: when the examiner flies an error such as a nose drop at glide entry, a stretched glide, a skidding gliding turn or a pitch-up after rollout, name it, explain the cause and give the fix.
skills.practice: Learn the 13 AFH descent errors with a 'what you see' and a fix for each, and have another CFI applicant fly them for you to call out [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, what target descent rate goes with a partial power descent?
options: 300 fpm
400 fpm
500 fpm
quiz.why: The target descent rate for a partial power descent should be 500 fpm [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

quiz.q: The minimum safe airspeed descent is normally flown at no more than what speed?
options: 1.3 VSO
1.2 VSO
Best glide speed
quiz.why: The AFM/POH airspeed for this descent is normally no greater than 1.3 VSO [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

quiz.q: Why does the nose tend to drop as soon as the throttle is closed in most airplanes?
options: The center of gravity shifts forward as the engine fuel flow drops off
Less slipstream over the tail reduces the tail-down force
P-factor increases at idle and pushes the nose down
Induced drag on the wing suddenly increases at idle
quiz.why: With less propeller slipstream over the horizontal stabilizer, tail-down force decreases and the nose tends to lower [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

quiz.q: Best glide airspeed occurs at which point?
options: The critical angle of attack
The maximum lift-to-drag ratio
The minimum sink airspeed
Maneuvering speed at gross weight
quiz.why: Best glide airspeed occurs at the highest lift-to-drag ratio, L/D [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

quiz.q: Compared with best glide, how does the AFH describe minimum sink speed?
options: A few knots slower, giving less distance
Equal to best glide in a headwind
The speed that gives the steepest glide
A few knots faster, giving more glide distance
quiz.why: Minimum sink is generally a few knots below best glide and results in less distance traveled but the most time aloft [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

quiz.q: In a power-off glide, which rudder pressure does the AFH say is likely needed to stay coordinated?
options: Slight right rudder
Slight left rudder
Firm right rudder
None at all
quiz.why: Built-in compensation for P-factor and slipstream remains with the power off, so slight left rudder is likely needed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three things the AFH says push the nose down in a gliding turn?
options: Adverse yaw from the down aileron
Excess rudder from light pressures
Nose-down stability, power off
Lift tilted with the bank
quiz.why: The three are the lift direction, excessive rudder and the airplane's power-off nose-down stability [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

quiz.q: Per the PHAK, how much power can carburetor heat cost?
options: Up to about 5 percent
None if the engine is warm
Up to 15 percent
About 25 percent
quiz.why: Carburetor heat can reduce engine power, sometimes up to 15 percent, because heated air is less dense [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say to do periodically in a long idle glide?
options: Cycle the carb heat off and on to check for ice
Lean the mixture to keep the plugs clean
Reduce the airspeed to cut down the excessive engine cooling
Advance the throttle and hold it for a few seconds
quiz.why: Advance the throttle periodically and sustain it for a few seconds to avoid excessive cooling, plug fouling and carb ice [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: Which item is first on the AFH list of descent errors?
options: Stretching the glide
Too little entry back pressure
Chasing the airspeed
Poor clearing for traffic
quiz.why: Failure to adequately clear for traffic in the turn direction or descent is listed first [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner closes the throttle and immediately lowers the nose to the glide picture. The airspeed rises 15 knots above best glide. Which two AFH errors does this combine?
options: Stretching the glide and chasing the airspeed indicator
Excess rudder in the recovery and poor clearing for traffic
Too little entry back pressure and not slowing to glide speed first
Cross-controlling and failing to hold a constant bank angle
final_quiz.why: Inadequate back pressure at entry gives an overly steep glide, and the nose went down before the airspeed slowed to glide speed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: Gliding toward a field that looks a little too far, your learner raises the nose to 'float' farther. What is the result, per the AFH?
options: A flatter path that reaches the field
No change, since only wind affects reach
A longer glide but higher descent rate
A shorter glide and a stall risk
final_quiz.why: Slowing below best glide increases drag and shortens the glide; stretching it can lead to landing short and to a stall [[24:83|AFH 3-22]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: Solo the learner's airplane is 250 pounds lighter than on your dual flights. How should the glide differ?
options: Slightly lower airspeed, same distance
Same airspeed, shorter distance
Higher airspeed, shorter distance
Same best glide speed, longer glide distance
final_quiz.why: Weight does not change glide distance at the right speed; the heavier airplane needs a higher airspeed, so the lighter one glides slower over the same distance and takes longer [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: In a 30° gliding right turn, the ball sits to the left and the learner is pressing hard on the right pedal while adding back pressure. What is the most serious concern?
options: A slip that will steepen the glide slightly
A skid that can develop into a spin
Overbanking from too much left aileron
Carb ice from the low power setting
final_quiz.why: Ball to the outside with rudder into the turn is a skid; excessive rudder in a gliding turn with back pressure can rapidly become a spin [[24:74|AFH 3-13]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: In a 50° gliding turn the nose drops and airspeed climbs. Your learner pulls hard on the yoke. What should you teach instead?
options: Add power before doing anything else
Reduce bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose
Add rudder into the turn to bring the nose up
Hold the bank and pull harder until airspeed stops rising
final_quiz.why: Recovering from nose-low steep bank with elevator alone only steepens the bank; reduce bank first, then increase pitch [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

final_quiz.q: A learner levels off from a 500 fpm practice glide by starting 50 feet above the target and wants to finish at cruise speed. She ends up 40 feet low. What does the AFH suggest?
options: Pull up harder at 50 feet without adding power
Use the 10 percent rule, which gives 50 feet
Start the level-off about 100 feet above
Add flaps to slow the descent first
final_quiz.why: For a 500 fpm descent with a final speed above glide speed, the AFH puts the lead at about 100 feet because the lead depends on both descent rate and the desired final airspeed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: Outside air is 10°C with high humidity. Your learner plans a 3,000 foot idle descent. What is the best plan for carburetor heat?
options: Wait for an RPM drop, then apply partial heat to save power
Full heat only during the final 500 feet
Full heat before closing the throttle, and keep it on
No heat, since the temperature is above freezing
final_quiz.why: With icing suspected and closed throttle planned, set full heat before closing the throttle and leave it on; partial heat can make things worse [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: During a long idle descent your learner's eyes never go to the engine gauges. What does the AIH suggest this indicates?
options: Fixation on the attitude indicator
Inattention, a natural result of fixation or boredom
Good outside scan, which needs no correction
Spatial disorientation beginning in the turn
final_quiz.why: Learners whose gaze never goes to the engine instruments might have a problem with inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]], and inattention is often a by-product of fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

final_quiz.q: After a long gliding turn in haze, the learner feels level but sees the altimeter unwinding, and pulls back. What is happening?
options: A graveyard spiral that the pull tightens
Somatogravic illusion from acceleration
The leans, which is harmless once the wings are level
Normal sink in a coordinated glide
final_quiz.why: In a prolonged turn the pilot can feel level while descending; pulling back tightens the spiral and increases altitude loss [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

final_quiz.q: Descending toward a nontowered airport for practice, which clearing technique does the PHAK give for the descent itself?
options: Gentle banks left and right, often enough to keep scanning
Rely on ADS-B traffic alerts and keep the wings level throughout
S-turns of 90° every two minutes
Clear once at the top, then hold heading
final_quiz.why: During climbs and descents with visual conditions, make gentle banks left and right at a frequency that permits continuous scanning [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies smooth glides but only to the left. What should you change?
options: Nothing, since the right turn is the same with power off
Add power in right turns to equalize the rudder need
Move on to spot landings to build confidence first
Add right gliding turns; one-direction proficiency is a listed error
final_quiz.why: Gaining proficiency in turns in only one direction is a listed turn error [[24:78|AFH 3-17]], and power-off rudder needs differ from powered flight [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: You want a distraction during descent practice that fits this Task. Which one comes straight from the AIH list?
options: Glide toward a field without looking at the airspeed
Descend 200 feet and hold it, then climb back
Spiral down 500 feet and roll out on a heading
Climb 200 feet and hold it, then descend 200 feet
final_quiz.why: The AIH distraction list includes having the learner climb 200 feet and maintain altitude, then descend 200 feet and maintain altitude [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: In a fast, slick airplane the learner closes the throttle and the nose dips by a degree before he catches it. Why does the AFH stress this more for fast airplanes?
options: Their stall speed rises at idle
Their trim cannot be changed with power off
They do not lose speed readily, so speed builds at once
They glide farther, so errors do not matter
final_quiz.why: Fast airplanes do not readily lose airspeed; any slight nose-down deviation gives an immediate airspeed increase [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

takeaways: Power sets how much energy you lose; pitch decides whether it comes off as altitude or airspeed.
Know the power, horizon pitch picture and instrument indications for each descent in your airplane; 500 fpm is the partial power target.
Glide entry: throttle closed, hold the nose until best glide, set the attitude, trim. Never stretch the glide.
Gliding turns need more back pressure and less rudder than you expect; release the pull on rollout.
Lead the level-off by about 10 percent of the descent rate, more when you want to end up faster.
Carb heat on before the throttle closes when icing is possible; clear the engine periodically on long descents.
Clear before and during descents with gentle banks, and know the 13 AFH errors with a fix for each.
cfi_notes: The AFH sets a 500 fpm target for a partial power descent [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] but uses 1,000 fpm in its level-off example on the same page [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Teach the AFM/POH descent speed and power with 500 fpm as the default target, and the 10 percent lead as a rule that works at any rate.

The 10 percent rule gives a 50 foot lead at 500 fpm, but the AFH puts the lead at about 100 feet for a 500 fpm practice glide that ends faster than glide speed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The two are consistent: the lead depends on descent rate and on the final airspeed wanted. Say both parts out loud.

The AFH glide entry holds altitude until best glide speed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. That is the training entry from cruise. Real engine failures at low altitude are taught in the emergency lessons; do not let this maneuver's altitude-hold become a habit near the ground.
The AFH says slight left rudder is likely in a glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], hedged with 'likely'. Confirm in your airplane before you teach it; some trainers need almost none.

The AFH covers gliding turns and climbing turns in detail [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] but says almost nothing specific about partial power descending turns. This lesson teaches them by application of the level turn and gliding turn principles; tell learners that is where the technique comes from.

The PHAK says to open the throttle for a few seconds now and then on closed-throttle descents [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]] and the AFH says the same for long glides [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Neither gives an interval; use the POH, and if it is silent, pick an altitude interval and teach it consistently.

The AFH asks for more back pressure in a gliding turn than in a straight glide, yet lists failure to lower the pitch attitude at gliding turn entry as an error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Application: both hold, since the nose goes slightly lower to keep glide speed, and back pressure keeps it from dropping further. Teach the attitude target, not the pressure, to avoid confusing learners.

The AIH's own distraction list includes a 200 foot climb and 200 foot descent [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], so this Task is a natural place to add distractions, but keep head-down ones out of turns because of the Coriolis risk [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

The PHAK notes that, after a propeller overspeed, the published best glide speed may not be the best speed for some airplanes [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]. Teach best glide as the normal glide, and leave that exception to emergency training with the AFM/POH.
gaps: The descent airspeed and power for a prolonged descent, the best glide speed and any minimum sink speed come from the AFM/POH; the handbooks give no numbers for a specific airplane.
The CFI ACS gives no numeric tolerance for this Task, and the AFH gives no bank angle for practice gliding turns.
No source gives an interval for clearing the engine in a long idle descent, or a cylinder head temperature limit; that is AFM/POH and engine manufacturer data.
The sources do not describe a right seat demonstration technique or how the descent sight picture looks from the right seat.
Partial power descending turns are not described step by step in the AFH; only gliding turns and climbing turns are.

activities.title: Which descent is it?
activities.intro: Tap a descent, then tap its description.

pairs.r: Normal en route descent, 500 fpm target
Nose high, power assisted, to clear obstacles
High drag, high airspeed, per the AFM/POH
Power off at best glide speed
Power off at any other speed

activities.title: Glide entry in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the glide entry steps in order (AFH 3-23, with the PHAK carb heat step), then tap Check.
steps: Carburetor heat on if icing conditions are suspected
Close the throttle; propeller control forward if equipped
Add back pressure to hold altitude as the nose tries to drop
Let the airspeed decrease to best glide speed
Set the glide pitch attitude on the natural horizon
Trim away the control pressure once the airspeed is stable

activities.title: Read the descent panel
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the round-gauge panel.

pins.label: Confirms the descent or glide airspeed
Shows the slightly nose-low pitch picture
Tells you when the level-off lead arrives
Its ball shows slip or skid in a gliding turn

activities.title: Descent numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your learner descends at 800 fpm toward 2,500 feet. Using the AFH 10 percent rule, how many feet above 2,500 should the level-off begin?
items.why: 800 x 0.10 = 80 feet. Use 10 percent of the descent rate as the lead [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

items.q: An airplane travels 9,000 feet forward while losing 1,000 feet. What is its glide ratio (to 1)?
items.why: 9,000 / 1,000 = 9, so 9 to 1. Glide ratio is distance traveled compared with altitude lost [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

items.q: With a 10 to 1 glide ratio in still air, how many nautical miles can the airplane glide from 4,000 feet AGL? (1 NM = 6,076 feet)
items.why: 4,000 x 10 = 40,000 feet. 40,000 / 6,076 = 6.58, about 6.6 NM. Glide ratio from the AFH example of 10 to 1 [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

items.q: You plan a partial power descent at the AFH target rate from 6,500 to 2,500 feet. How many minutes does it take?

activities.title: True or false: the engine in long descents
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Carburetor ice can build unnoticed in a reduced-power descent until power is added.
cards.why: True. It is particularly dangerous during reduced-power descents [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

cards.s: When carburetor icing is suspected, partial carburetor heat is the safest setting.
cards.why: False. If ice is present, partial heat or too little time on heat might make it worse; with icing suspected and closed throttle planned, use full heat [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

cards.s: A long idle glide can cause spark plug fouling as well as excessive engine cooling.
cards.why: True. Periodically advance the throttle for a few seconds [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

cards.s: High-speed descents can shock cool the engine with abrupt temperature changes.
cards.why: True. They provide excess cooling air [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

cards.s: In a descent from high altitude the mixture should be leaned further to prevent detonation.
cards.why: False. The mixture must be enriched, or it may become too lean and cause detonation [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

activities.title: When does the error show up?
activities.intro: Tap each AFH error, then tap the part of the maneuver where you would first see it.

items.t: Inadequate back pressure, overly steep glide
Lowering the nose before reaching glide speed
Stretching the glide with back pressure
Not lowering the pitch as the bank goes in
Excessive rudder during recovery from the turn
Inadequate pitch control recovering from a straight glide

activities.title: Down from 6,000 feet, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFI. Your learner is in a carbureted high-wing trainer at 6,000 feet on a damp, cool morning, about to practice a straight glide, gliding turns and a level-off at 4,000 feet.

steps.s: The learner reaches for the throttle to start the glide.
options: Set partial carb heat to save power
Close it now; add carb heat if the engine roughens
Carb heat full on first, then close the throttle
Skip carb heat; icing needs freezing air
steps.why: With icing suspected and closed throttle planned, full carburetor heat goes on before the throttle is closed [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

steps.s: As the descent starts, the learner looks only at the airspeed indicator.
options: Gentle banks left and right to keep scanning
Fine, as long as best glide is held
Ask the learner to call traffic only at level-off
Turn on the landing light and continue
steps.why: During descents, gentle banks left and right allow continuous scanning [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]], and chasing the airspeed is a listed error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

steps.s: In the first gliding turn the airspeed climbs 10 knots and the nose sits low.
options: Roll out and start again
Add rudder into the turn
Add power to hold the speed
Add a little more back pressure than in the straight glide
steps.why: Gliding turns need more back pressure than a straight glide because three factors push the nose down [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

steps.s: On rollout the nose comes up and the speed drops below best glide.
options: Add right rudder
Normal; the trim will fix it
Lower the flaps
Release the back pressure added for the turn
steps.why: Back pressure applied in the turn must be decreased on recovery, or the airplane pitches up and loses airspeed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

steps.s: Descending at 500 fpm toward 4,000 feet, the learner wants to finish at cruise speed.
options: Begin at 4,050 with no power until level
Begin about 100 feet above with cruise power and pitch control
Begin at 4,000 and pull up firmly
Begin 300 feet above with full power
steps.why: For 500 fpm with a final speed above glide speed, start about 100 feet above, add cruise power and control the pitch [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
